notes.meaning: God calls Israel His own children. So they must not copy their neighbors, who cut their skin or shaved the front of their heads to mourn the dead. Those customs came from idol worship and showed grief with no hope. God's people still grieve, but they have a living Father in heaven, so they need not mourn like people who have no hope.

Here is the reason for verse 1. Israel is "holy," which means set apart for God. God chose them as His treasured people. He did not choose them because they were better than others, but so that by His kindness they would become His. Because they belonged to God, they were not to lower themselves by taking up the customs of idol worshipers.

"Detestable" here means any food God called unclean, meaning not fit to eat. These food rules marked Israel out as a separate people. They also kept Israel from sharing meals and mixing closely with their idol-worshiping neighbors. Matthew Henry notes that the gospel makes plain these food laws no longer bind Christians (1 Timothy 4:4).

God gives a generous list of animals Israel may eat. It includes farm animals and many kinds of wild game, like deer and antelope. With so much allowed, the people had no reason to complain about the few foods that were off limits. Some of the wild animals named are hard to identify today.

Here is a simple test for land animals. An animal was clean if it had a hoof split in two and chewed the cud. Chewing the cud means bringing food back up to chew it again, as cows and sheep do. Animals like these feed on plants and were thought to be very wholesome food.

An animal had to pass both parts of the test. The camel, the rabbit, and the rock badger seem to chew the cud, but they have paws, not split hooves. The pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud. All of these were unclean, and Israel was not even to touch their dead bodies.

For water creatures there is one rule. Anything with both fins and scales could be eaten, so most fish were allowed. Creatures without them were unclean. That meant shellfish like crabs, clams, and lobsters were off limits, and so were eels and catfish.
Israel could eat any clean bird. No general test is given for birds. Instead, the forbidden ones are named in the verses that follow. Any bird not on that list was allowed.

The list of forbidden birds begins. Most of them, like eagles, vultures, and kites, hunt other animals or eat dead ones. The exact Hebrew bird names are sometimes hard to match with birds we know today.

The list goes on with ravens, owls, hawks, and others. Matthew Henry points out that few of these birds are eaten even today. The Geneva Notes say these rules about food were meant to teach Israel to seek a deeper, inner purity before God.

The list ends with water birds like the cormorant, stork, and heron, plus the hoopoe and the bat. Again, these are mostly birds that hunt or scavenge. God was marking out what His holy people should and should not eat.
Winged insects were also unclean and were not to be eaten. Some translations put it as winged creatures that crawl along the ground.
The section on birds closes as it began, with permission. Every clean bird may be eaten. God's list of what is forbidden is short compared with all that He allows.

Israel was not to eat an animal that died on its own, because its blood had not been drained. Blood stood for life, which belongs to God. Such meat could be given or sold to an outsider passing through, which shows these food laws were for Israel only, not for all people. The ban on cooking a young goat in its mother's milk was most likely aimed at a pagan religious custom.

A tithe means a tenth. Each year Israel was to set aside a full and honest tenth of the harvest, with no shortcuts. Many commentators say this is a second tithe, separate from the tithe given to the Levites. The owners set this one aside themselves, so God trusted them to be honest.

The people were to eat this tithe in a joyful meal at the place God would choose for His worship, later Jerusalem. The goal was to teach them to "fear the LORD," which here means a glad, holy respect while enjoying God's company. Coming often to worship would also help keep them from idol customs.

Some people would live far from the place of worship, especially after God blessed them with a large harvest. They could sell the tithe at home and carry the money in a bag instead. This shows how practical and kind God's commands are.

At the place of worship they could buy whatever food and drink they liked and hold a feast before God with their whole family. Using God's gifts cheerfully, with self-control, honors Him. This verse shows that God's law cared for His people's joy and comfort.

The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve in worship, and they had no farmland of their own. So the people must not forget them but share these feasts with them. God made His ministers depend on the people. That gave the ministers reason to work for the people's spiritual good, and the people reason to support them.

Every third year the tithe stayed in the hometown. It was used to feed the Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows, people who had no land of their own. The years were counted from the seventh-year rest for the land, so this happened in the third and sixth years. God promises to bless those who work hard and give freely.
